newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian court kills state tax powers.
newsitem.headline: Australian court kills state tax powers.

text.p: Australia's highest court on Tuesday struck out state rights to tax alcohol, tobacco and petrol, threatening to wipe out billions of dollars of revenue.
In a four to three majority ruling, the High Court of Australia ruled that business franchise fees were in fact an excise, which only the national government can raise under Australia's constitution.
"We are conscious that this judgement has the most serious implications for the revenues of the states and territories," said the four majority judges, including chief judge Gerard Brennan.

Constitutional experts said the national government would have to swiftly levy its own taxes to replace the state charges, which account for about 16 percent of the income raised by Australia's six states and two territories.
"It is clear that it's a big loss for the states," lawyer George Williams told reporters outside the court.

"The result from that will be that the states, in order to maintain their approximately A$5.0 billion (US$3.7 billion) of revenue base will need to turn to the Commonwealth," said Williams, a constitutional expert at the Australian National University.
Tuesday's judgement, on a challenge by two tobacco retailers, only applies specifically to tobacco franchise fees in New South Wales state, but will flow on to other states and charges.
"What this judgement does is it confirms the trend, particularly since 1949, that the states are really kept out of the area of raising revenue from indirect taxes on goods," Williams said.

The ruling is likely to see prices for petrol, alcohol and tobacco rise in some states, because the national government cannot levy different rates in different areas and is expected to set its rates at the highest existing levels.
Currently, the franchise fees vary between states and one, Queensland, has no charge at all on petrol.
Williams said Tuesday's ruling also ended state hopes for a consumption tax on the sale of goods and services. "At the state level that's gone. That's not an option," he said.
"That's one of the things the states hoped for. They bet a lot on the outcome of this case, and they've decisively lost in their attempt to gain access to those broader forms of taxation."
The national government will now have to negotiate a rescue package with states to replace their lost income.

"There'll be a long negotiating process of working out exactly how much revenue was raised and then of course how it is to be distributed again," said Deborah Cass, a constitutional expert at the Australian National University who watched the case with Williams.

Williams and Cass said the states and territories would have to stop collecting the levies immediately, but added that the national government could backdate its replacement package to date from Tuesday.
The states had argued that the turnover-based franchise fee was simply a licence fee for the right to sell the products.
But the court's majority judgement ruled it was clearly an excise and therefore invalid under the constitution.
